Confucius identified seventy-seven disciples proficient in the six arts, categorizing them by virtue (Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhong Gong), political skill (Ran You, Ji Lu), eloquence (Zaiwo, Zigong), and erudition (Ziyou, Zixia). He noted individual traits: Zhuan Sun was extreme, Zeng Shen slow, Gao Chai stupid, Zhong You rude, and Yan Hui poor. Zigong, rejecting fate, became a successful merchant. Confucius respected figures like Laozi, Zang Boyu, Yan Zhongping, Laolaizi, Zichan, and Meng Gongchuo, and praised others from earlier eras.
Yan Hui (Yan Yuan), thirty years younger than Confucius, was praised for virtue, living frugally without changing his joy. Confucius said he restrained himself to conform to etiquette, was not stupid, and shared a philosophy of serving when employed and hiding when not. Yan Hui died prematurely at twenty-nine, causing Confucius great grief. Duke Ai of Lu was told Yan Hui was the best learner, never transferring anger or repeating mistakes.
Min Ziqian, fifteen years younger, was deemed exceptionally filial, avoiding official service. Ran Boniu suffered an incurable disease; Confucius lamented his fate. Zhong Gong, asked about governance, was advised to be courteous and cautious; Confucius deemed him fit for high office despite his humble father. Ran Qiu, twenty-nine years younger, managed military affairs for the Ji family; Confucius encouraged his timidity. Zilu (Zhong You), nine years younger, was bold and straightforward, initially bullying Confucius but later becoming a disciple. Confucius taught him to prioritize righteousness over bravery, and he died in Wei during a rebellion, tying his hat before death.
Zaiwo, eloquent, questioned the three-year mourning period, suggesting one year sufficed; Confucius rebuked him for lacking benevolence. Zaiwo later died in a rebellion in Qi. Zigong, thirty-one years younger, was articulate and wealthy. Confucius compared him to a vessel and praised his humility. Zigong’s diplomatic mission saved Lu, disrupted Qi, destroyed Wu, strengthened Jin, and enabled Yue’s dominance, altering the balance of power among states.
Ziyou, forty-five years younger, governed Wucheng with music and ritual; Confucius joked about using a “knife to kill a chicken” but later praised him. Zixia, forty-four years younger, discussed the Book of Songs with Confucius, who noted his slight deficiency. After Confucius’s death, Zixia taught in Hexi. Zizhang, forty-eight years younger, learned about gaining office through caution and about achieving success through loyalty and respect. Zeng Shen, forty-six years younger, understood filial piety and wrote the Book of Filial Piety.
Other disciples included Tantai Mieming, initially judged poorly by appearance but later renowned; Mi Zijian, praised as a gentleman; Yuan Xian, who valued poverty over shame; Gongye Chang, married to Confucius’s daughter; Nangong Kuo, praised for morality; and Gao Chai, deemed stupid. Youruo, resembling Confucius, was briefly treated as a teacher but failed to answer questions. His half-sister Wei Zifu gained favor with Emperor Wu of Han, leading Wei Qing to adopt the surname Wei. As a youth, he served as a servant and shepherd, enduring mistreatment from his half-brothers. Mencius, a student of Zisi’s disciples, failed to gain favor with King Xuan of Qi or King Hui of Liang, who found his ideals impractical. During an era of reforms—where states like Qin, Chu, Wei, and Qi thrived through figures like Shang Yang, Wu Qi, and Sun Bin—Mencius advocated ancient virtues, which did not align with the prevailing strategies of alliances and warfare. Among the eight types of government officials in "Hong Fan," the third type is sacrificial officials. Sacrifice is performed to show filial piety, serve ancestors, and understand gods. Sacrifices are widespread among surrounding ethnic minorities, and even animals like jackals and otters perform them. The sage king established laws and rituals for sacrifices. If a spirit is single-minded, respectful, solemn, and wise, gods may come to him, designating men as 觋 and women as witches to reach the gods and provide sacrifices. Descendants of previous sages who understand mountains, rivers, worship etiquette, and divine affairs become wizards; those who understand pure-color livestock for seasonal sacrifices, sacrificial locations, and godly origins are called sect members. Thus, there are officials above the gods and below the people, each managing their own affairs without confusion. The people and gods have different roles, respecting each other without offense, so gods send good luck, people follow natural order, disasters do not come, and needs are met.
After the young Emperor Wu weakened, nine members of the Li family rebelled, causing chaos among people and spirits. Families worshiped witches and made unrestrained sacrifices, defiling the gods, who considered them unclean. Good luck did not come, disasters occurred frequently, and lives could not be completed. Zhuanxu accepted this and ordered Nan Zhengzhong to master astronomy to entrust the gods and Huo Zhengli to master geography to entrust the people, restoring normalcy without violating or defiling the gods. Since the Gonggong family dominated Kyushu, his son Julong could pacify the water and soil and was worshiped as the land god after death. Lieshan ruled the world, and his son Zhu produced hundreds of grains and was worshiped as a grain god after death. Worshiping land and grain gods in the countryside has a very early origin.
"Yu Shu" says Shun observed the Xuanji Jade Scale to organize the sun, moon, five stars, and seven political affairs. He offered sacrifices to heaven, six sects, mountains, rivers, and gods everywhere. He collected auspicious jade from princes, uncles, sons, and men, chose an auspicious month and day, met with pastors and guardians of princes, and awarded the jade. In February each year, he inspected the east and arrived at Daizong (Mount Tai), burning firewood and sacrificing by rank. He harmonized the four seasons, months, and dates, unified rhythm and weights, revised the five rituals and music, and used three silks, two life and one death as stinging rituals. In May, he inspected Nanyue (Hengshan); in August, Huashan; in November, Beiyue (Hengshan), all with the same etiquette as Daizong. Zhongyue is Mount Song. Inspections occurred every five years. Dayu continued this system.

Thirteen generations later, Emperor Wuding got Fu Yue as prime minister, reviving the Yin Dynasty, and Wuding was named Gaozong. A pheasant crowed on a tripod, frightening Wuding. Zu Ji said to cultivate virtue. Wuding obeyed, and the throne remained peaceful. Five generations later, Emperor Yi neglected the gods and was struck by thunder and died. Three generations later, Emperor Zhou became promiscuous, and King Wu crusaded against him. From this, it seems that initially there was respect for the gods, but later it gradually declined.

The emperor's places for worshiping heaven were called Mingtang and Piyong; princes' places were called Pangong. Sacrifices to Hou Ji in the suburbs matched offerings to heaven, and sacrifices to King Wen in the Mingtang clan matched offerings to heaven. Within the four seas, everyone assisted in sacrifices according to their positions. The emperor sacrificed to the world's famous mountains and rivers, inviting gods to appease them, all in order. Princes only sacrificed to famous mountains and rivers within their territory, officials sacrificed to five places including gates and stoves, and common people only sacrificed to ancestors. The uses of property, money, cloth, and silk were not recorded before the Xia and Yin dynasties. Jiang Taigong established currency circulation for the Zhou Dynasty: gold was one inch square and weighed one catty; coins were round with square holes, using baht as weight; cloth was two feet two inches wide and four feet long per piece. Currency was considered more precious than gold, sharper than a knife, smoother than spring water, more dispersed than cloth, and more able to gather than silk. After Jiang Taigong retreated to Qi, he implemented this system. Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan of Qi by establishing standards for measuring weight, noting that grain prices fluctuated with harvests and that goods varied in value based on demand. He warned that without governance, hoarding merchants would exploit the people, raising prices a hundredfold. A country with ten thousand cars needed merchants worth ten thousand gold to buy them, as profits were hidden. By consuming what was produced, expenses could be met, but hunger arose when grain was hoarded. The monarch should levy low prices when grain was abundant and distribute at high prices when scarce, adjusting supply and demand to stabilize prices. A town of ten thousand households should have a collection of ten thousand bells and millions of strings of money. Farming required abundant equipment and seeds in spring and summer, preventing big merchants from robbing the people. Duke Huan used Qi to unite the princes and become an overlord.
More than a hundred years later, King Jing of Zhou worried that money was too light and planned to cast large coins. Duke Shan Mu advised against it, arguing that when disasters came, property and currency should be weighed to save the people. If money was light, heavy money should be created for use, with both types circulating together. Abolishing light money for heavy money would cause the people to lose wealth, leading to shortages and flight. King Jing ignored this and made large coins with "actual goods" engraved, which benefited the people. When Qin annexed the world, currency was divided into two classes: gold measured in yi, and copper coins shaped like Zhou money with "ban liang" inscribed, weighing half a liang. Pearls, jade, turtles, shells, silver, and tin were decorations, not currency, and changed value arbitrarily. After the Han rose, they found Qin coins heavy and ordered pod coins instead, with gold returning to the weekly system of kilograms. Those who pursued profits hoarded goods, causing prices to skyrocket—rice reached ten thousand gold per stone, and a horse was worth one hundred gold. Emperor Gaozu ordered merchants not to wear silk or ride carriages and increased taxes to frustrate them. During Emperor Xiaohui and Queen Gao's reign, laws on merchants were relaxed, but their descendants could not become officials.
In the fifth year of Emperor Xiaowen's reign, four baht coins were minted with "banliang" on the front, and the law on stealing money was abolished, allowing people to mint coins freely. Jia Yi remonstrated, arguing that coining money with copper and tin led to doping for profit, and even daily tattooing could not stop it. He noted that coins varied by county—some light, some heavy—causing confusion. People abandoned farming to mine copper, increasing illegal money without increasing grain. He proposed collecting copper to prevent scattering, which would bring seven blessings: reducing tattooing crimes, eliminating fake money, returning miners to farming, balancing money and goods, distinguishing noble from humble, enriching the government while impoverishing merchants, and competing with the Xiongnu. The emperor did not listen. Wu State minted coins in Shanhuo, becoming richer than the emperor, and later rebelled. Deng Tong, a great official, minted coins and became wealthier than kings. Their money spread worldwide.
During Emperor Wu's reign, wars with the Xiongnu and campaigns in the southwest and Guangdong drained resources. The government used money to buy titles and exempt people from punishment, leading to official chaos. Gongsun Hong, as prime minister, used moral principles to restrain ministers, while Zhang Tang used harsh laws. The Yellow River flooded, costing billions. The emperor discussed changing coins to supplement expenses, using white deer skin for leather coins worth 400,000 yuan and silver-tin platinum coins. The government destroyed half-liang coins and recast three baht coins, punishing secret minting with death. Shu Guo Xianyang and Kong Wei were appointed as great agricultural ministers to manage salt and iron, while Sang Hongyang, a merchant's son, became favored. The government set up salt and iron officials, taxed merchants, and confiscated hidden property. The rich went bankrupt, and the government grew richer through salt and iron. The emperor built Kunming Pool and Bailiang Fortress, expanding palaces. The government used confiscated land and slaves for farming, and the grain transported to the capital reached four million shi.
After Wang Mang became regent, he changed the Han system, creating various coins like big coins, deed-knife coins, and wrong-knife coins. He later abolished these and introduced treasure goods, including gold, silver, turtle, shell, money, and cloth coins. He established six types of coins, each with different values, and implemented credit and five equalizations to control prices. He set up officials in Chang'an and five capitals to manage trade, taxing craftsmen and merchants. He also regulated wine production, with the government making wine and taking seven-tenths of the profit. Despite these measures, the people suffered, and many broke the law. Wang Mang executed those who made private coins and moved critics to remote areas. The corvee was heavy, and droughts and locusts caused trouble. Officials collected taxes privately, and the rich could not protect themselves, leading to widespread banditry. The Han army killed Wang Mang four years after the conquest of Zhutu Xiyong. Two years later, Shizu restored the five-baht coin and eliminated harsh laws. The text praises ancient methods of regulating commodities and prices, noting that during Emperor Xiaowu's time, expenses were met without increasing taxes, but under Wang Mang, the system failed, and the people suffered.

Emperor Yuan of Han, son of Emperor Xuan, was made prince at age eight. He was generous and respected Confucianism, often criticizing his father's reliance on legal officials and harsh punishments. Emperor Xuan warned that Confucian scholars would disrupt the Han dynasty's system, which blended kingly and hegemonic rule. Though Emperor Xuan favored another son, he ultimately kept Emperor Yuan as heir due to loyalty to his mother.
Upon ascending the throne in 48 BCE, Emperor Yuan honored his mother and wife as empresses, granted amnesty, and distributed rewards. He issued edicts addressing natural disasters, earthquakes, and famines, ordering relief efforts, tax exemptions, and land grants to the poor. He reduced palace expenses, dismissed entertainers, and lent public lands to farmers. He also sent officials to inspect local governance and seek wise men.
In subsequent years, Emperor Yuan continued responding to crises: earthquakes, floods, plagues, and famines led to further tax exemptions, amnesties, and relief measures. He abolished certain laws, reduced palace staff, and encouraged remonstrance. He appointed Confucian scholars like Gong Yu and Kuang Heng as officials, but his indecisiveness weakened the state. He also dealt with rebellions, such as the Xiqiang uprising, and military campaigns against the Xiongnu, including the execution of Zhizhi Chanyu.
Emperor Yuan's reign saw numerous natural disasters and social unrest. He repeatedly issued edicts blaming himself for poor governance and seeking advice. He reformed policies, including abolishing the death penalty for certain family crimes and reducing corvée labor. He also established his own mausoleum, Weiling, and ordered that no new migrants be forced to settle there.
Emperor Yuan died in 33 BCE after 16 years of rule. Ban Gu's commentary notes that Emperor Yuan was talented in music and calligraphy, respected Confucianism, and appointed many Confucian scholars as officials. However, his indecisiveness and adherence to literary principles led to the decline of Emperor Xuan's achievements. Despite this, his generosity, thrift, and gentle edicts reflected the legacy of ancient wise kings.

Emperor Hui of the Han Dynasty, son of Emperor Gaozu and Empress Lu, became crown prince in the second year of Gaozu's reign. After Gaozu's death in April of the twelfth year, Hui ascended the throne on May 17, with his mother becoming empress dowager. He issued decrees rewarding subjects with titles and promoting officials based on service length: Zhonglang and Langzhong officials serving six years received third-level promotions, those serving four years received second-level promotions, and various other officials received specific rewards. Those who organized Gaozu's funeral received monetary rewards based on salary, and those who built his mausoleum received gold. Land rent was reduced to one tax per fifteen people. Certain officials and their families were exempted from corvée labor except military tax. Princes were ordered to build Gaozu's ancestral temple.
In the first year of his reign, King Liu Ruyi of Zhao died. Subjects could atone for capital crimes with money. Commoners received title promotions. Chang'an city construction began. In the second year, King Hui of Qi presented Chengyang County to increase Princess Lu Yuan's territory. Two dragons appeared in Lanling, an earthquake struck Longxi, drought occurred, and Yanghou Liu Zhong and Prime Minister Xiao He died. In the third year, 146,000 workers built Chang'an for thirty days. A Liu family princess married the Xiongnu Shanyu. The King of Minyue was titled King of East China Sea, and 20,000 princes and slaves built Chang'an. A fire broke out in royal stables, and Zhao Tuo of South Vietnam paid tribute. In the fourth year, Zhang Ao's daughter became queen. Filial and loyal sages were exempted from corvée. The emperor held a crown ceremony with amnesty, abolished restrictive Qin laws, and fires occurred in Changle and Weiyang Palaces. In the fifth year, unusual weather included thunder and fruit blossoming in winter. Another 145,000 workers built Chang'an. Severe drought struck, Prime Minister Cao Shen died, and Chang'an city was completed. In the sixth year, King Fei of Qi died. Titles could be bought, and unmarried women aged fifteen to thirty were fined. Fan Kuai died, and the west city and Aocang were built. In the seventh year, chariot officers were sent to Xingyang. Solar eclipses occurred, and Emperor Hui died in Weiyang Palace on August 12, buried in Anling on September 5. Ban Gu commented that Hui was kind and respectful but fell short of saintliness due to Empress Lu's actions.

Empress Gao, of the Lu family, was the mother of Emperor Hui and assisted Emperor Gaozu in pacifying the realm. After Emperor Hui ascended, she became the Queen Mother. She arranged for her granddaughter, the daughter of Princess Lu Yuan, to be the Queen, who had no children, so a son from a harem beauty was made prince. Upon Emperor Hui's death, this prince became emperor, but due to his youth, Empress Dowager Lu ruled in his stead, granting amnesty and promoting her relatives: four of her brother's sons were made kings, and six others were made princes.
In the first year of her reign, she abolished harsh laws and rewarded the people. She established officials to encourage filial piety. In the second year, she ordered merit rankings for princes to be preserved in the ancestral temple. Natural events occurred: earthquakes, solar eclipses, and floods. In the fourth year, the young emperor, aware he was not the Queen's biological son, complained and was imprisoned. The Empress Dowager replaced him with Liu Hong, King of Hengshan. In the fifth year, Wei Tuo, King of Nanyue, declared himself emperor. In the sixth year, there was a general amnesty and construction at Changling. The Xiongnu invaded in the seventh year, and several kings died or were imprisoned. In the eighth year, Empress Lu died in Weiyang Palace.
After her death, Lu Lu and Lu Chan, holding military and political power, plotted rebellion. Zhu Xuhou Liu Zhang, son of King Qi, learned of this and coordinated with his brother, King Qi, and officials Zhou Bo and Chen Ping to counter them. King Qi raised an army, and General Guan Ying, sent to stop him, instead allied with him. Zhou Bo, using deception, gained control of the Northern Army by tricking Lu Lu into surrendering his command. Lu Chan, attempting a coup, was killed by Liu Zhang. The Lu family was then exterminated. The ministers, believing the young emperor and his brothers were not Emperor Hui's sons, killed them and enthroned Emperor Wen. Ban Gu noted that under Empress Gao, the world was peaceful, with reduced warfare and punishments, allowing the people to prosper in farming.
